summary: This experimental document extends IKEv2 so endpoints can use more than one authentication exchange, with different or the same mechanisms. For example, the client host can be authenticated with a certificate and then the user with EAP, possibly by servers in different administrative domains.

eli5.summary: Entering a building might need both your badge and your password. This lets secure connections ask for more than one kind of proof, one after another.

questions: how to authenticate a host and user separately in ikev2
what are the ikev2 multiple auth notifications
subtitle: Performing two or more authentication exchanges in sequence during key establishment.

tldr.problem: The Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2) protocol normally authenticates each party using a single mechanism, such as a certificate or shared secret. Some scenarios require verifying multiple credentials, such as authenticating both a host device and the user on it, or authenticating to both an access provider and a service provider.
tldr.mechanism: This extension allows two notification payloads, MULTIPLE_AUTH_SUPPORTED and ANOTHER_AUTH_FOLLOWS, to signal when a peer wants to perform additional authentication exchanges after an initial one succeeds.
tldr.outcome: Peers can now authenticate using different methods in sequence, such as certificate authentication of the host followed by EAP authentication of the user, or multiple authentications to different backend servers.

today: RFC 4739 is an Experimental protocol. It remains the specification for performing multiple authentication exchanges in IKEv2, though it is not a standard. Implementations that need multi-factor authentication in IKEv2 follow this design.

sections.title: Motivation for Multiple Authentication
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2) protocol establishes secure connections by authenticating the parties involved. Normally, each endpoint authenticates itself to the other using one mechanism: a digital certificate, a shared secret key, or an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method.

However, some real-world scenarios need more than one proof of identity. For example, when a VPN provider hosts access for a third party, the client might need to authenticate to both the access provider (for billing) and the third party (for authorization to access their network). Or a corporate gateway might require authenticating both the host computer and the current user on it.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you need to prove who you are in two ways: maybe your company badge and your password, or a key card and a code. This adds that to secure connections.

sections.title: How Multiple Authentication Works
sections.content:
Both peers announce support for this extension by sending a MULTIPLE_AUTH_SUPPORTED notification in the initial IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH messages. If both sides support it, either endpoint can signal that it wishes another authentication exchange by including an ANOTHER_AUTH_FOLLOWS notification in an IKE_AUTH message.

When this notification is sent, the sending peer will include a new identity payload in its next message and repeat the authentication exchange. The IKE_AUTH phase only succeeds if every individual authentication exchange completes successfully. Each exchange can use the same authentication method or different ones.
sections.eli5: The two peers say 'we both support doing this twice'. When one wants another proof, it sends a signal, then the whole dance repeats with new credentials.

sections.title: Authentication Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes four practical scenarios. First, the responder authenticates with a certificate, then the initiator authenticates with EAP (for example, the user logs in with a username and password). Second, both sides authenticate with certificates, then the initiator authenticates with EAP. Third, the initiator sends two different certificates to prove two different identities. Fourth, the responder sends two different certificates.

When multiple EAP authentications occur, they are separate independent conversations, not a sequence within one EAP exchange. Each may involve a different EAP server, and they may even be terminated by different backend authentication servers in different administrative domains, such as a network access provider and an internet service provider.
sections.eli5: You might prove you are an employee (with a certificate), then prove you are Alice (with a password). Or reverse the order. The system is flexible about the order and the methods used each time.

sections.title: Notification Payloads
sections.content:
The extension defines two new IKEv2 notification types. The MULTIPLE_AUTH_SUPPORTED notification (type 16404) is sent with no associated data, signaling capability. The ANOTHER_AUTH_FOLLOWS notification (type 16405) is also sent with no data, but it is placed in an IKE_AUTH message that contains an AUTH payload, indicating the sender wants to start another authentication exchange.

Both notifications set the Protocol ID and SPI Size fields to zero, as they apply to the entire security association, not a specific protocol or connection.
sections.eli5: Two simple signals are added to IKEv2 messages. One says 'I support doing this twice'. The other says 'I want to do it again'.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC notes that a key difference from standard IKEv2 is that the responder reveals its identity before all of the initiator's authentication exchanges have completed. In normal IKEv2, the responder authenticates the initiator before showing its own identity (except when EAP is used). With multiple authentications, the responder must reveal its identity during the first exchange, even if the initiator has more authentications to perform later.

This change does not eliminate security; rather, it shifts the trust model. The responder must be comfortable with this exposure. The RFC recommends that implementations carefully consider the implications when choosing to use this extension, and that readers pay special attention to the security properties of EAP methods that do not generate shared keys.
sections.eli5: There is one tradeoff: the server shows who it is before all client proofs are done. This is a deliberate choice, and the RFC says to think about it carefully.
